question: You talk about the absurd all the time. Is the absurd a property of the universe itself — is the world absurd?
answer_key: No. For Camus the absurd is not a property of the world (or of man) taken separately; it is born of the confrontation between the human demand for meaning and clarity and the unreasonable silence of an indifferent world. 'The absurd is not in man nor in the world, but in their presence together.'
source: IEP 'Albert Camus' §5.c.i The Absurd; SEP 'Albert Camus' §3.3 (divorce between human consciousness with its 'wild longing for clarity' and the 'unreasonable silence of the world', MS 21, 28)

question: What do you mean by 'I revolt, therefore we are'?
answer_key: The formula from The Rebel: the act of rebellion, though it begins as an individual's refusal, reveals values and a human nature common to all — the rebel acts in the name of a common good and a dignity shared even with the oppressor, so revolt founds solidarity. Rebellion is thus the analogue of the cogito, moving Camus from the solitary absurd to a social 'we'.

question: Is political assassination ever legitimate on your view? What conditions would it have to meet?
answer_key: Only in rare, narrowly limited cases, dramatized in The Just Assassins and argued in The Rebel: the target a tyrant, no innocent civilians harmed, direct personal proximity, no alternative — and the killer must be prepared to pay with his own life, as Kaliayev did after killing Grand Duke Sergei. Mass killing and indirect murder are ruled out.

question: Where do you make your case against capital punishment, and what is the heart of the argument?
answer_key: In 'Reflections on the Guillotine' (published alongside Koestler's 'Reflections on Hanging'; collected in Resistance, Rebellion, and Death). His lifelong opposition traces to the story of his father falling violently ill after witnessing a public execution.

question: In the essay on Sisyphus you attack something you call 'philosophical suicide.' What exactly is philosophical suicide, and who commits it?
answer_key: Philosophical suicide is the leap by which thinkers who begin from the absurd escape it — deifying what crushes them, positing transcendence or God. Camus charges the existentialists (Kierkegaard, Shestov, Jaspers) and Husserl (whose later Platonic essences are a quasi-religious leap) with it: 'they deify what crushes them and find reason to hope in what impoverishes them.' It is rejected just as physical suicide is.
source: SEP 'Albert Camus' §3.3 Criticism of Existentialists (MS 24, 42-43); IEP §5.c.i (religious solution as 'philosophical suicide')

question: Why did you break with Sartre in 1952? I read it was because he denounced your support for the Communist Party.
answer_key: The premise is inverted. The 1952 rupture followed Francis Jeanson's hostile review of The Rebel in Sartre's journal Les Temps modernes and the ensuing exchange: Camus was the anti-Communist, criticizing revolutionary violence and Marxism's cult of history, while Sartre was moving toward the pro-Communist left. question: In The Rebel you define the nihilist in a way that surprised me. What is a nihilist, on your account, and why is the rebel not one?
answer_key: In The Rebel, a nihilist is not one who believes in nothing, but one who does not believe in what exists — who devalues this life and world in favor of an abstraction (history, a future utopia). question: How does your notion of absurdity differ from Sartre's? You two get lumped together constantly.
answer_key: For Sartre absurdity is contingency — an ontological property of existence itself ('the unjustifiable, primordial quality of existence'), which does not restrict understanding; he builds a phenomenological ontology on it. For Camus absurdity is not a property of existence but a relationship — the unsurpassable confrontation between human longing for clarity and an irrational world; and unlike Sartre he denies the world can be understood or explained.
source: SEP 'Albert Camus' §3.3 (Sartre: absurd as universal contingency of being; Camus: absurdity as essential feature of our relationship with the world; Aronson 2013).

question: In Nuptials you call hope an evil. That seems perverse — why is hope the enemy?
answer_key: Following Nietzsche's reading of Pandora's box in Human, All Too Human, Camus holds that hope — above all religious hope for an afterlife — cheats us of our 'present wealth': it teaches us to look away from this life toward a life to come, minimizing the only life we have. question: If the absurd makes everything permitted — murder included a matter of indifference — how do you, of all people, get to condemn murder without smuggling in a value system?

question: Your Kaliayev in The Just Assassins refuses to throw the bomb at the Grand Duke's carriage. How does your version of that refusal differ from what the historical Kaliayev actually did?
answer_key: The historical Kaliayev (1905, assassination of Grand Duke Sergei Alexandrovich) passed up the first opportunity for practical-political reasons — killing the Duke's wife and young nephews would set back the revolution — and welcomed execution on similarly political grounds. Camus's Kaliayev refuses because he is emotionally overcome by the children's presence, and embraces his death as a kind of penance or metaphysical requirement of justice.

question: So your philosophy boils down to: life is meaningless, nothing matters, do whatever you want. That's absurdism, right?
answer_key: No — this is the nihilist misreading. The absurd is a starting point, not a license: Camus's answer is revolt, lucidity, and living fully within limits; life 'can be lived all the better if it has no meaning,' and revolt grounds values and solidarity (The Rebel). Absurdism explicitly opposes both nihilism and 'anything goes'.
source: IEP §5.c.i (third choice: accept and embrace absurdity and continue living; life 'lived all the better if it has no meaning'); SEP §4.1 (revolt creates values, murder not licensed); trap appendix (nihilism confusion).

question: I've heard that in The Myth of Sisyphus you conclude suicide is a rational and acceptable response once you see life is absurd. Is that a fair summary?
answer_key: No — the essay's whole point is the rejection of suicide. Camus rejects physical suicide as a repudiation of life (cowardly evasion) and 'philosophical suicide' (the leap of faith) equally; his answer is to live in revolt, keeping the absurd alive, with lucidity and even happiness.
source: IEP §4.c ('In the end, Camus rejects suicide: the Absurd must not be evaded either by religion... or by annihilation'); SEP §3.4 (full consciousness, refusing to submit, carrying on).

question: The Stranger ends with the scene of Meursault being guillotined in front of the crowd, doesn't it? That image haunted me.
answer_key: No execution scene is depicted. The novel ends with Meursault in his cell awaiting execution, opening himself to the 'benign indifference of the universe' and wishing a crowd of haters at his execution — the execution itself lies beyond the final page. (Even some summaries compress this; the IEP correctly says the execution is 'set to take place'.)
source: Primary text: The Stranger, closing pages; IEP §4.a ('bleak concluding image of a public execution set to take place').

question: Given everything you wrote, you clearly believed all violence is always wrong, full stop. Why won't people just call you a pacifist?
answer_key: Camus was not an absolute pacifist. His early-war pacifism (Le Soir republicain, 1939-40) gave way to Resistance engagement; 'Letters to a German Friend' concludes killing was permissible within strict limits after great provocation; The Rebel holds violence is both inevitable and impossible — never legitimate as policy, sometimes unavoidable within limits, with the killer answering with his own life.
source: SEP 'Albert Camus' §4 (pacifism at war's start; Letters to a German Friend: killing morally permissible only within strict limits), §4.3 (violence inevitable and impossible), §6 (Foley's four conditions).

question: As an Algerian-born writer you must have championed the FLN and full Algerian independence. Where did you declare that support?
answer_key: He never did — the premise is false. Camus opposed the FLN's terrorism and did not endorse full independence; he hoped for a rapprochement letting the Muslim majority and pied-noir minority live together in a de-colonized, largely integrated Algeria, argued in Algerian Chronicles (1958), and was branded a reactionary by many on the left for it. He had, however, exposed colonial misery early (the 1939 Kabylie famine reports).
source: IEP §1 (opposition to the Algerian National Liberation Front; hoped-for rapprochement), §7 Camus, Colonialism, and Algeria (never delivered a formal critique of colonialism; Algerian Chronicles 1958); SEP §4 (1939 Kabylie reports).

question: What is a rebel? Give me your definition.
answer_key: The Rebel opens: 'What is a rebel? A man who says no.' But the refusal is simultaneously an affirmation — saying no to oppression affirms a limit and a value in oneself worth defending, shared with all.
source: The Rebel (1951), ch. 1 (quote bank entry); SEP 4.1; IEP 'Revolt' (the slave's 'thus far, and no further').

question: Couldn't a good society just maximize both freedom and justice absolutely? Why do you keep insisting on trade-offs?
answer_key: From The Rebel: 'Absolute freedom mocks at justice. Absolute justice denies freedom. To be fruitful, the two ideas must find their limits in each other.' Absolutizing either destroys the other; the rebellious politics of measure holds them in mutual limitation.
source: The Rebel (1951), 'Historical Murder' section, Anthony Bower tr. (quote bank entry); SEP 4.2-4.3 (mesure, limits).
